case_title: Prosecutor v. Naser Orić — superior responsibility for detention crimes
question: Has it been established beyond reasonable doubt that the commander of the Srebrenica armed forces was criminally responsible as a superior, under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, for failing to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb detainees in Srebrenica between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993?
facts: Between September 1992 and March 1993, Serbs were detained in Srebrenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the police station and at a building behind the Srebrenica Municipal Building. The Trial Chamber found that crimes of murder and cruel treatment were committed against the detainees during two periods: from 24 September to 16 October 1992, and from 15 December 1992 to 20 March 1993. It found that the Military Police was responsible for the occurrence of all these crimes, and that the Military Police was subordinated to the commander of the Srebrenica armed forces, through the successive Chiefs of Staff, only after 27 November 1992. The persons who physically committed the crimes were not found to be members of the Military Police or to be directly subordinated to the commander. The head of the Military Police after 27 November 1992 was found to be subordinated to the commander and responsible for the crimes committed between December 1992 and March 1993. The Trial Chamber's findings on the commander's mental state concerned his knowledge of, or reason to know of, the crimes committed in the two detention facilities. The Trial Chamber convicted him under Article 7(3) for failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment committed between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993, and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment.
holding: In its Judgement of 3 July 2008, the ICTY Appeals Chamber reversed the convictions and acquitted the accused of all charges. The Trial Chamber had identified only one culpable subordinate, the head of the Military Police, but had failed to resolve whether and on what basis that subordinate incurred criminal responsibility, and had failed to make a finding on whether the accused knew or had reason to know that this subordinate was about to engage, or had engaged, in criminal conduct. Without these findings the convictions under Article 7(3) could not stand. The Prosecution's alternative basis, superior responsibility for unidentified guards, had not been pleaded in the Indictment.
confidence_reasoning: The facts as given directly track the Trial Chamber's findings and conviction. The legal principles cited (Rome Statute Art. 28, customary IHL Rule 153, AP I Art. 86(2)) are materially equivalent to the ICTY Statute Art. 7(3) standard for command responsibility. The only gap is that the arguments cite the Rome Statute rather than the ICTY Statute, but the substantive test is the same. Confidence is not higher because the question asks whether it was established 'beyond reasonable doubt' — a factual determination by the Trial Chamber — and we have only the summary of findings, not the full evidentiary record.

verdict.conclusion: Yes. The commander was criminally responsible under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute for failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb detainees between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993. The Trial Chamber's findings establish the requisite superior-subordinate relationship, the commander's knowledge or reason to know, and his failure to take necessary and reasonable measures.
verdict.reasoning: The facts as given establish that: (1) after 27 November 1992 the Military Police was subordinated to the commander through successive Chiefs of Staff, creating effective command and control during the charged period (27 December 1992 – 20 March 1993); (2) the head of the Military Police was subordinated to the commander and responsible for the crimes in that period; (3) the crimes occurred in detention facilities overseen by the Military Police; and (4) the Trial Chamber convicted the commander under Article 7(3) after assessing his mental state. The surviving arguments correctly identify the legal elements — effective control (Rome Statute Art. 28(a), customary IHL Rule 153), knowledge or reason to know (Rome Statute Art. 28(a)(i), customary IHL Rule 153), and failure to take necessary and reasonable measures (Rome Statute Art. 28(a)(ii), customary IHL Rule 153, AP I Art. 86(2)) — and apply them to the established facts. The fact that the physical perpetrators were not formal Military Police members does not break the nexus, as effective control over the Military Police, which oversaw the detention sites, suffices (Rome Statute Art. 28, customary IHL Rule 153, AP I Art. 86(2)). No objections were filed to challenge these arguments.

arguments.claim: The commander exercised effective command and control over the Military Police during the period 27 December 1992 – 20 March 1993, establishing the requisite superior‑subordinate relationship for command responsibility.
arguments.reasoning: The Trial Chamber found that after 27 November 1992 the Military Police was subordinated to the commander through successive Chiefs of Staff. Under international law a superior must have effective command and control over the forces whose conduct is at issue; the Rome Statute expressly links criminal responsibility to such effective authority.

citations.quoted_text: A military commander or person effectively acting as a military commander shall be criminally responsible for crimes within the jurisdiction of the Court committed by forces under his or her effective command and control, or effective authority and control as the case may be, as a result of his or her failure to exercise control properly over such forces, where: (i) That military commander or person either knew or, owing to the circumstances at the time, should have known that the forces were committing or about to commit such crimes; and (ii) That military commander or person failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures within his or her power to prevent or repress their commission or to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution.

arguments.claim: The fact that the actual perpetrators were not members of the Military Police does not defeat command responsibility because liability attaches to the commander for crimes committed by forces under his effective control, irrespective of direct orders.
arguments.reasoning: Article 28(b) of the Rome Statute extends superior responsibility to any subordinate relationship, not limited to formal military command. Thus, the lack of direct subordination of the perpetrators is immaterial to liability.
